Since `_exchangeRateStored` and `_getCashPrior` all use `totalUnderlying`, direct transfers are orphaned from supply accounting, and a token with a fee-on-transfer where `_doTransferOut` forwards `amount` but the recipient gets `amount - fee` is silently accounted as if full amount left. In `_seize`, `totalSupply` and `accountTokens` are reduced by `protocolSeizeTokens` while `totalReserves += protocolSeizeAmount`, which is consistent with `totalUnderlying` unchanged — so seized tokens' underlying value stays in reserves only if `exchangeRateStored` recomputes consistently; on mErc20Host with `doTransfer=false` external accrual, the underlying was never sent so accounting depends entirely on `totalUnderlying` bookkeeping.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker uses a fee-on-transfer underlying (listed by admin) to mint: `_doTransferIn` returns net amount and `totalUnderlying += net`, so mint is correct. Redeem: `_doTransferOut` sends `amount`, recipient gets `amount - fee`, but `totalUnderlying -= amount`. The fee is taken from the contract, meaning the redemption user absorbs the fee while remaining suppliers' `totalUnderlying`-based rate is unaffected — which understates loss only if fee exceeds expectation. More direct: any direct ERC20 transfer to the market leaves `balanceOf > totalUnderlying`; that underlying is unredeemable and permanently stuck.
hypotheses.impact: Directly-sent underlying is permanently locked; with non-standard transfer tokens the accounting drifts and some suppliers cannot exit at the rate they expect.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute `_getCashPrior()` from `IERC20(underlying).balanceOf(address(this))` minus any pending transfers, or add a reconciliation/skim function; disallow fee-on-transfer/rebasing underlyings at the Operator level.

hypotheses.title: performExtensionCall for actionType == 2 can be called by any msg.sender without an outflow allowance, and outPerChain is written with wrong id and value (`_amount` unset)
hypotheses.description: In `performExtensionCall`, the `actionType == 2` branch calls `_borrow(msg.sender, amount, false)` which accrues debt to `msg.sender`, but `msg.sender` does not need to be an authorized caller or have any prior credit — the function only requires `msg.value >= gasFees`. The `_borrow` flow does not charge the underlying and does not transfer out, so this becomes a free entry to open debt and, critically, writes `acc[dstChainId].outPerChain[msg.sender] += _amount` where `_amount = amount` in this branch. Then the on-chain debt is never tracked back to that outPerChain entry. On L2 the extension will credit the sender based on `outPerChain`, but here the host records the debt without transferring underlying. Combined with `_checkOutflow` summing across the caller's amount only once, a user can open a borrow position while the outflow check computes only `amount`.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker calls `performExtensionCall(1, X, dstChainId)` (withdraw) for amount `X`, which increments `outPerChain[msg.sender]` by X but reduces only supply (that's OK). Then calls `performExtensionCall(2, Y, dstChainId)` for arbitrary Y (bounded only by `_getCashPrior`, i.e. open debt up to available cash), which writes `outPerChain[msg.sender] += Y`. On the extension chain the same user holds both signatures and can claim both withdraw and borrow, but the debt is registered against msg.sender here — yet the outflow balance for the sender is already used up, allowing more debt than intended on the destination.
hypotheses.impact: Debt is created against the borrower's mTokens without any liquidation check; a user can borrow on the destination chain without previous collateral on the source, potentially undercollateralized repayment on extension.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `actionType == 2`, do not decrement `_getCashPrior`/`totalUnderlying` without transferring; verify `beforeMTokenBorrow` actually requires liquidity for the same account (it does) — but currently `_checkOutflow` is on `amount` only while the debt is created; ensure per-chain accounting is bound to the proof at claim time.

hypotheses.title: BatchSubmitter.verifyInput failure reverts entire batch although events catch per-op; and journals indexed by startIndex while hashes/amounts arrays are zero-based — length mismatch is unchecked
hypotheses.description: `batchProcess` uses `length = data.initHashes.length` to bound the loop, but indexes `journals[data.startIndex + i]`, `data.amounts[i]`, `data.minAmountsOut[i]`, `data.receivers[i]`, `data.mTokens[i]`, `data.selectors[i]` — no check that all these arrays have at least `length` entries or that `startIndex + length <= journals.length`. An under-sized array (e.g., `receivers` shorter than `initHashes`) causes an out-of-bounds revert, so the whole batch reverts even though the per-op `try/catch` was designed to let failures be reported. Conversely, an oversized `journals` array with `startIndex` pointing beyond a mixed set means some journals processed earlier/later than `initHashes` imply. The proof is verified once for `journalData`, but the individual journals are re-encoded into `singleJournal = [journals[startIndex+i]]` and passed to the mToken/gateway with an empty seal and no further proof verification; authorization then rests solely on the mToken/gateway internals trusting `msg.sender` (the BatchSubmitter), so any journal content between `startIndex` and `startIndex+length` is treated as pre-authorized.
hypotheses.attackPath:
1. A compromised/misconfigured PROOF_FORWARDER crafts `journalData` with extra journals and a `startIndex` that selects journals not intended by the submitting protocol, while `initHashes`/`amounts` arrays match the fake set.
2. The verifier's `verifyInput(journalData, seal)` passes because the image was built for the whole array; per-op calls use `""` seal and rely on caller trust.
3. mToken/gateway processes foreign journals (e.g., minting to the attacker's `receivers[i]`) under the BatchSubmitter's identity.
hypotheses.impact: Journal-to-action binding is bypassable within the batch: the proof is only over the blob, not over which subset is executed with which amounts; and an attacker who can influence one forwarder action can execute additional journal entries. Also, mismatched array lengths cause batch-wide reverts (DoS of whatever batching the forwarder needs).
hypotheses.recommendation: Enforce `startIndex + length <= journals.length` and `length == receivers.length == amounts.length == minAmountsOut.length == mTokens.length == selectors.length`. Bind the executed subset/amounts to the proof (encode them into the verified journal, or have the mToken verify the real seal per op).

hypotheses.title: Blacklister._removeFromBlacklistList silently leaves list intact if address not found
hypotheses.description: `_removeFromBlacklistList` loops over `_blacklistedList` and removes on first match but does nothing if the address is not found (no revert). Because blacklist/unblacklist are independent of the `isBlacklisted` mapping, if the list ever desynchronises from the mapping (e.g., a duplicate push is impossible, but external state or future refactor), `getBlacklistedAddresses()` can diverge from `isBlacklisted`. The for loop also iterates the full list per removal; combined with no dedupe on `_addToBlacklist` beyond the mapping check, the view `getBlacklistedAddresses()` (used by external integrators/UI) can become inconsistent with the authoritative `isBlacklisted(user)`.
hypotheses.attackPath: A user blacklisted, then the same address pushed again only if mapping is reset bypassing `blacklist` — not directly exploitable; more practically, callers relying on `getBlacklistedAddresses()` may miss a user if any code path leaves a stale mapping. The primary risk is DoS from an unbounded loop as the blacklist grows, blocking unblacklisting.
hypotheses.impact: Unblacklisting gas grows linearly; a large blacklist makes `unblacklist` expensive, and any list/mapping drift causes integrators to see wrong sets.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use an index mapping (address => index+1) for O(1) removal and keep the array and mapping strictly in sync; revert if the address is not found.

hypotheses.title: mTokenGateway.whitelist/gasFee can be bypassed via supplyOnHost if wrapper contract is whitelisted
hypotheses.description:
`supplyOnHost` enforces `onlyAllowedUser(msg.sender)` and `ifNotBlacklisted(msg.sender)` and `ifNotBlacklisted(receiver)`, plus `require(msg.value >= gasFee)`. The `WrapAndSupply.wrapAndSupplyOnExtensionMarket` contract calls `supplyOnHost` and only forwards `msg.value` implicitly — it never adds `gasFee`, and it has no whitelist/blacklist awareness for the actual user. If the wrapper is whitelisted (likely, to enable native-asset supply), any user can supply through it while bypassing the whitelist gate on their own EOA (the check sees the wrapper), and the wrapper does not check `receiver` bl  
against blacklist — `supplyOnHost` does check `receiver`, so that part holds, but the `gasFee` requirement makes `WrapAndSupply` always revert unless the user overpays ETH to the wrapper and the wrapper forgets to forward it.
hypotheses.attackPath: Non-whitelisted user calls `WrapAndSupply.wrapAndSupplyOnExtensionMarket` (if wrapper whitelisted); whitelist check passes for wrapper, not user. Or user pays exactly `msg.value` for wrapping; `supplyOnHost` requires `msg.value >= gasFee`, and the wrapper forwards `msg.value` unchanged, so a value exactly equal to wrap amount fails — but there is no forwarding logic shown to add gasFee, so the entire path reverts whenever gasFee > 0.
hypotheses.impact: Whitelist bypass for supplies, and/or the native-asset supply wrapper is permanently broken whenever `gasFee > 0`.
hypotheses.recommendation: Have `WrapAndSupply` accept and forward `msg.value = amount + gasFee`, and consider having `supplyOnHost` read the real end-user (e.g. via a trusted caller mapping) rather than `msg.sender`.

hypotheses.title: _grantReward uses ImToken(token) for reward token, but reward token may not implement ImToken.balanceOf semantics
hypotheses.description: `_grantReward` reads `ImToken(token).balanceOf(address(this))` and calls `ImToken(token).transfer(user, amount)`. The reward token is whitelisted by owner (`whitelistToken`) and need not be an mToken, but the code treats it as ImToken. `ImToken.transfer` returns bool; a normal ERC20 return works, but the check `require(status)` will revert for tokens not returning bool (though here it decodes as ImToken). More critically, `_claim` sets `accountState.rewardAccrued = _grantReward(...)` which returns 0 on success; if insufficient balance, it returns the original amount leaving the accrued balance — meaning users can never be paid if the distributor is underfunded, silently. The owner can drain via `grantReward` (no balance check) leaving others unclaimable.
hypotheses.attackPath: Owner calls `grantReward` with an amount exceeding the distributor's balance of the token (it only checks `isRewardToken`). `_grantReward` sees amount > remaining so it returns amount, silently not transferring; but no funds moved. Later claimants find the distributor underfunded. This is owner trust, so lower severity. However: via `_claim`, if `amount > remaining`, it returns `amount` (unchanged), so `rewardAccrued` is not zeroed — the user's claim silently fails while the operator already updated indices, but that behavior is intentional partial-claim.
hypotheses.impact: Users may be unable to claim while balances run out; but no direct theft.
hypotheses.recommendation: Revert on transfer failure / underfunding rather than returning silently.

hypotheses.title: _repayExternal checks amount validity after executing repay (effect before validation)
hypotheses.description: In `_repayExternal`, `_repayBehalf(receiver, repayAmount, false)` is executed first, mutating `accountBorrows`, `totalBorrows`, and `totalUnderlying`, and then the code checks `require(repayAmount > 0)` and `require(actualRepayAmount <= _accAmountIn - acc[...])`. A zero-repay or over-accrual is only caught after the borrow state has been changed. Since these are in the same transaction, the revert undoes state, so the direct impact is limited, but the ordering violates the effects-before-external-call discipline used everywhere else and makes the function fragile: any future refactor that moves the repay into a separate call, or a token whose transfer triggers a callback before the require, could leave inconsistent borrow accounting.
hypotheses.attackPath: A caller supplies `repayAmount = 0` with a valid journal where `_accAmountIn` is nonzero; `_repay` runs its state changes and emits `RepayBorrow`, then `require(repayAmount > 0)` reverts the whole tx. With a hook-capable underlying used in `doTransfer=false` path this is benign, but the reversed order means validations cannot rely on state not having advanced.
hypotheses.impact: Risk of inconsistent accounting if underlying or operator is ever refactored to defer checks; currently a revert-guarded footgun rather than immediate loss.
hypotheses.recommendation: Move the `require` validations for `repayAmount` and the accrual bound before calling `_repayBehalf`.

hypotheses.title: blacklist() is not guarded by ifNotBlacklisted and can re-blacklist addresses; but the real issue: unblacklist after re-add creates duplicate list entries / stale list
hypotheses.description: `unblacklist` sets `isBlacklisted[user] = false` and calls `_removeFromBlacklistList`, which finds *one* entry and swaps/pops it. If, via the rest of the system, `_addToBlacklist` is reachable while a user is already blacklisted (the guard in `blacklist()` blocks this today, but `_addToBlacklist` is also reachable indirectly through future functions or a stored-state mismatch), duplicates could exist. More concretely, the array swap-and-pop in `_removeFromBlacklistList` iterates and `break`s on the *first* match; combined with the fact that membership in `_blacklistedList` and `isBlacklisted` are mutated in different functions with no cross-check, `getBlacklistedAddresses()` can return a list that no longer matches `isBlacklisted` after a blacklisted-then-unblacklisted-then-re-added cycle at a different index. However, the strongest concrete issue is the ordering in `unblacklist`: it clears the mapping before removing from the array, so `_removeFromBlacklistList` must succeed for consistency; if `user` is somehow not in the array (state desync from a failed external write, or removal of a duplicate), the array retains `user` forever while `isBlacklisted` is false, and `getBlacklistedAddresses()` permanently lists an un-blacklisted address, and re-blacklisting it pushes a duplicate that a future unblacklist only partially removes.
hypotheses.attackPath:
1. Guardian blacklists `u`; array `[u]`, flag true.
2. Guardian unblacklists `u`; array `[]`, flag false.
3. Guardian blacklists `u` again; array `[u]`, flag true.
4. Guardian unblacklists `u`; array `[]` — fine. But if any integration path (`_addToBlacklist`) were ever called twice before an unblacklist (e.g. new owner functions in part 2), removing once leaves a ghost entry, and the loop breaks on the first match so the duplicate persists, causing `getBlacklistedAddresses()` to over-report/drift.
hypotheses.impact: Any consumer trusting `getBlacklistedAddresses()` (dashboards, off-chain proofs, UI) sees addresses that aren't blacklisted, breaking integration / allowing perceived blacklisted addresses to appear live while funds flow, and duplication can desync the guardian's tooling.
hypotheses.recommendation: Have `unblacklist` revert if `_removeFromBlacklistList` didn't find the entry, and add an internal guard in `_addToBlacklist` against duplicates (or assert on the array membership before adding).

hypotheses.title: EverclearBridge sendMsg does not check token.transferFrom and does not verify market is the token holder
hypotheses.description: `sendMsg` approves the `everclearFeeAdapter` for `params.amount` and calls `newIntent`, but it never pulls tokens from the Rebalancer itself. It relies on the Rebalancer's prior `safeApprove(_msg.token, _bridge, _amount)` and the fee adapter pulling via allowance. When `_extractedAmount > params.amount`, the bridge transfers the excess back to `_market` from its own balance; however if the fee adapter does not pull exactly `params.amount` or the approve allowance is left over, the leftover allowance persists (SafeApprove resets to 0 before next set, but leftover bridge-held balance after `extractForRebalancing` may not reconcile). More importantly, the market is trusted blindly via `_market` and the excess-return transfer could fail or mismatch the actual extracted amount accounting.
hypotheses.attackPath: Rebalancer calls with an amount larger than `params.amount`; the bridge sends `params.amount` to Everclear and returns the difference to `_market`, but if the adapter charges differently or the transfer-from is skipped, tokens can remain stranded in the bridge or be returned incorrectly, desynchronising the market's extraction accounting.
hypotheses.impact: Stranded or misdirected tokens, and market accounting drift versus actual balances.
hypotheses.recommendation: Measure actual `token.balanceOf(address(this))` before and after calls to determine amounts moved, and transfer leftovers deterministically; validate the market and use checked balance deltas.

hypotheses.title: mTokenGateway.outHere can be called by proof forwarder for another user's sender without L1Inclusion and drains accAmountOut
hypotheses.description: `outHere` skips `_verifyProof` entirely when `msg.sender` has `PROOF_BATCH_FORWARDER`, and `_outHere` only checks `_checkSender(msg.sender, _sender)` which permits the forwarder role. However, `_checkSender` also permits `allowedCallers[srcSender][msgSender]`. Combined with the temporary `receiver = _sender;` overwrite in `_outHere`, funds always go to `_sender`. BatchSubmitter calls `outHere(encodedJournal, "", singleAmount, data.receivers[i])` with `encodedJournal` wrapping a single journal it accepts from chain data. If the forwarder is malicious or the journal is crafted for another user, funds are sent to `_sender` (who the journal declares) rather than `receiver`. The `accAmountOut[_sender]` accounting check `_accAmountOut - accAmountOut[_sender] >= amount` only validates against the same user's history, so a forwarder can't drain another user — but for any smart contract callers setting `allowedCallers`, the flow is unbounded by L1 inclusion.
hypotheses.attackPath: A contract/user sets `allowedCallers[themselves][forwarder] = true` for legitimate reasons; the forwarder now can submit arbitrary journals naming that user as `_sender` without `_verifyProof`, using a made-up high `_accAmountOut` — but the second check `_accAmountOut - accAmountOut[_sender] >= amount` limits to the difference. However, once a legitimate proof raised `_accAmountOut` for the user but funds were already paid elsewhere, the forwarder can replay journals with a fabricated `_accAmountOut`, effectively draining any balance remaining.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized release of underlying for users whose journals have been partially processed; loss to gateway liquidity, since `accAmountOut` can be inflated by the forwarder itself.
hypotheses.recommendation: Enforce `ifNotBlacklisted`/`onlyAllowedUser` against the actual `_sender` and, if `msg.sender` is a forwarder in `allowedCallers`, require the amount to be authenticated in a signed L1 journal; also make the temporary `receiver = _sender` override respect the caller's intent.

hypotheses.title: `_repayExternal` uses `outPerChain` sender debit but `_accAmountIn` allowance key is `acc[_chainId].inPerChain[_sender]` while `_repayBehalf` changes state before the amount check
hypotheses.description: `_repayExternal` calls `_repayBehalf(receiver, repayAmount, false)` before the amount bound check, which reduces `totalBorrows` and decrements the borrower's principal. The check `require(actualRepayAmount <= _accAmountIn - acc[_chainId].inPerChain[_sender])` happens after; if the check fails the whole tx reverts (OK), but if it passes, only `actualRepayAmount` is added to `inPerChain`. `actualRepayAmount` may be less than `repayAmount` (if `repayAmount` exceeds the debt, `__repay` will underflow at `accountBorrowsPrev - actualRepayAmount` and revert), so the effective accounting is subtle. Worse, `repayAmount` is delivered to `__repay` as `type(uint256).max`-sensitive only when caller uses it explicitly; here `repayAmount` is bounded by proof allowance but is required to be >0 only after the state update (a `mErc20Host_AmountNotValid` revert exists post-call, not pre-call). That is a wasted gas bubble, not a loss, but combined with off-by-one in `inPerChain` accumulation across multiple journals, the same journal allowance can be reused.
hypotheses.attackPath: Two journals with the same `(chainId, _sender, _accAmountIn, acc.inPerChain)` can each satisfy `repayAmount <= _accAmountIn - inPerChain` because `inPerChain` is only incremented after the repay; the update happens correctly in sequence though. However, the check is against `_accAmountIn` per journal, not against a running global cap, so the proof's `_accAmountIn` can be spammed with multiple identical entries — each satisfying the per-journal check — whenever `_decodeJournals` returns duplicates.
hypotheses.impact: Replays/multiple journals with the same `_accAmountIn` each pass independently; `inPerChain` grows monotonically so the same proof can't be reused across calls, but within a single transaction the batch is bound only by `computeSum(repayAmount)`. Sender-accounted `inPerChain` per chain is the only invariant.
hypotheses.recommendation: Validate `repayAmount > 0` before the external call, and validate the aggregate of `repayAmounts` against a proof-level total.

hypotheses.title: `Operator.enterMarkets` has no cap on accountAssets length; user can enter all markets and then exitMarket is O(n) with external calls in loop — DoS
hypotheses.description: `_getHypotheticalAccountLiquidity` iterates `accountAssets[account]` and calls `ImToken(_asset).getAccountSnapshot` plus the oracle's `getUnderlyingPrice` for each. `enterMarkets` has no maxAssets cap ("capped by maxAssets" comment is stale — no maxAssets implemented). An attacker can call `enterMarkets` with all listed markets, growing `accountAssets`. However this is their own array, and the cost is their own — not a griefing of others. `exitMarket` is O(n) with external calls, but only for that user. Borrow/redeem for a user with a huge `accountAssets` list will run out of gas and lock their funds.
hypotheses.attackPath: A user (or via `mint` auto-entering markets one by one) accumulates membership in many markets. Since the protocol can list many markets, `beforeMTokenRedeem` → `_beforeRedeem` → `_getHypotheticalAccountLiquidity(redeemer, ...)` iterates the whole list and calls oracle for each. As markets are listed by owner over time and the user auto-enters each via `enterMarketsWithSender` (called during `__mint`), their `accountAssets` grows; eventually redeem reverts due to gas limit and the user cannot withdraw collateral.
hypotheses.impact: Withdraw (redeem/borrow) DoS for users holding many markets; funds cannot be redeemed.
hypotheses.recommendation: Reintroduce a `maxAssets` cap in `_activateMarket`/`enterMarkets`.

hypotheses.title: `claimMalda(address)` uses `allMarkets` snapshot without deprecation/market filtering
hypotheses.description: `claimMalda(address holder)` iterates `allMarkets` and calls `_claim`, which requires `markets[mToken].isListed` — trivially true for all markets in the array. For a deprecated market the supply/borrow notify path still executes. Because deprecated markets set `reserveFactorMantissa == 1e18` but are not removed from `allMarkets`, claim still processes them; more critically if any market is ever de-listed (there is no de-list function currently), the require would revert, bricking the single-arg `claimMalda` for all users. The `getUSDValueForAllMarkets()` function correctly skips with `if (_isDeprecated(...)) continue;` but claim does not.
hypotheses.attackPath: Owner (or future guardian) never de-lists today, so not currently triggerable; but `reserveFactorMantissa` can be set to `1e18` on a market, making `_isDeprecated` true. The claim path still updates borrow index and distributes, so depreciation does not actually prevent claim distribution as intended, causing emissions from deprecated markets.
hypotheses.impact: Continued reward accrual/distribution from deprecated markets, effectively diluting active-market rewards.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `_claim`, skip markets where `_isDeprecated(mToken)` is true, matching `getUSDValueForAllMarkets`.
